title: Hooks for LinkedIn Video: 40 Openers That Make the Swipe Pause

# Hooks for LinkedIn Video: 40 Openers That Make the Swipe Pause

At 0:02, someone scrolling LinkedIn has already decided whether your video deserves the next sentence. A polished edit cannot rescue an opening that arrives late.

![Three Hook Lab hooks for one video](https://uploads.postiz.com/8cLEoX1RU8.png)

This page gives you 40 ready-to-use hooks for LinkedIn video, plus a simple way to choose one, test it, and turn it into a short script. Replace the bracketed details with your own proof.

## For founders and product teams

1. “We built [product] because [old way] broke at [specific moment].”
2. “The feature customers ask for first is not the feature that keeps them.”
3. “Here’s the customer question that changed our roadmap.”
4. “We stopped calling this a [category]. Here’s why.”
5. “Before you add another feature, watch where users quit.”

## For sales and client work

6. “The deal did not stall because of price.”
7. “A prospect said ‘send me more information.’ Here’s what I should have asked instead.”
8. “This one question turns a vague discovery call into a real conversation.”
9. “If your proposal starts with your company, rewrite page one.”
10. “The fastest way to lose a buyer is to solve the wrong problem beautifully.”

## For managers and team leads

11. “Your team may not need another meeting; it may need one clearer decision.”
12. “I can tell a project is drifting from the first update.”
13. “The phrase ‘let’s circle back’ is hiding a decision nobody owns.”
14. “A good one-on-one starts before either person joins the call.”
15. “If feedback surprises someone, the process failed before the conversation.”

## For career and job-search advice

16. “Your resume is not losing to better candidates; it may be losing to a vague first line.”
17. “Before you apply to another role, answer this question out loud.”
18. “The interview answer I would stop giving immediately is this one.”
19. “A career pivot looks risky until you name the skill you already carry.”
20. “Don’t say you are a strategic thinker. Start with this proof instead.”

## For consultants and service businesses

21. “Clients do not hire a process. They hire relief from a specific expensive problem.”
22. “The most useful sentence in my proposal is not the scope.”
23. “If every client asks for a discount, check this part of your offer.”
24. “Here’s how I explain a complex service in one breath.”
25. “A testimonial becomes persuasive when it includes the moment before the work started.”

## For marketing and content teams

26. “The post that got ignored had the right idea and the wrong first sentence.”
27. “Stop opening your video with ‘Hi, I’m [name].’ Open with the tension instead.”
28. “Your audience does not need more tips. It needs a reason this tip matters today.”
29. “The best case study hook starts with what almost went wrong.”
30. “If the headline could belong to any company, it will feel like an ad.”

## For operations, finance, and analytics

31. “This spreadsheet does not have a data problem. It has an ownership problem.”
32. “The metric moved, but the business did not improve. Here’s the difference.”
33. “Before you automate a workflow, time this one handoff.”
34. “The cost nobody puts in the budget is the wait between decisions.”
35. “One dashboard number can look healthy while the work underneath is stuck.”

## For technical experts and builders

36. “The bug was not in the code we changed.”
37. “Most technical explanations lose people before the first diagram.”
38. “We replaced [tool or process] after one failure kept repeating.”
39. “The useful question is not ‘Can we build it?’ It is ‘What happens when it fails?’”
40. “Here is the technical trade-off I would explain before anyone approves this plan.”

## Pick the hook that matches the video

A LinkedIn video hook should make one promise, not introduce your full topic. Pick the type that fits the material:

- Use a **contrarian hook** when you can challenge a familiar habit and explain the exception.
- Use a **mistake hook** when the viewer can recognize an avoidable error.
- Use a **scene hook** when you have a real meeting, decision, launch, or failure to walk through.
- Use a **question hook** when the answer is useful enough to earn the next 20 seconds.
- Use a **proof hook** when you can show the work, the process, or a specific before-and-after without inflating the result.

Write the spoken line first. Then add on-screen text that is shorter than the spoken line and carries the tension: “The proposal mistake,” “The stalled deal,” or “The metric that lied.” Do not make the text merely repeat every word.

## Test the first three seconds

Record two versions of the same video with the same middle and ending. Change only the opening line and on-screen text. Watch each version with the sound off, then with the sound on. Ask a colleague who fits your audience to say what they expect the video to answer after the first three seconds.

Keep the version whose promise is clearest. If viewers cannot predict the point, the hook is too broad. If they can predict the whole answer immediately, add a more specific tension: the mistake, the moment, the trade-off, or the question that changed the outcome.

A simple 30-second shape is: 0–3 seconds for the hook, 3–10 for the situation, 10–22 for the explanation or steps, and 22–30 for the next action. The hook earns attention; the rest has to deliver the promise.

## FAQ

### Should a LinkedIn video hook sound formal?

No. It should sound like a clear spoken sentence a professional would actually say. Specific beats formal: name the decision, mistake, constraint, or question.

### Can I use a question as the hook?

Yes, when the answer is not obvious and the video answers it promptly. “How do I grow?” is broad; “Why did this proposal lose after a strong first call?” sets a usable expectation.

### How many hooks should I write for one video?

Write at least three. One may be a question, one a mistake, and one a contrarian angle. Then choose the one that best matches the proof you can show in the video.

### What if I do not have a dramatic story?

Use a small, real moment: a sentence from a meeting, a decision in a project, a confusing metric, or a repeatable mistake. Precision creates interest without manufactured drama.

## What the tool returns

Here is a published example of the kind of input and output Hook Lab returns:

**You send:** "Hooks for a 30s TikTok about why most people quit the gym in January — energetic, for beginners."

**You get back (shortened):**
- **Positioning:** "The gym isn't the problem — your first week is." You own the beginner-who-keeps-quitting angle.
- **Hooks (5+, each with spoken line + on-screen text + type):**
  1. *Contrarian* — 🗣 "Stop going to the gym every day." / 🖥 "Day 1 is where you quit"
  2. *Question* — 🗣 "Why does everyone quit by January 20th?" / 🖥 "The January 20th wall"
  3. *Mistake* — 🗣 "You're not lazy. You're doing week one wrong." / 🖥 "Week 1 mistake"
- **Recommended pick:** #3, with one line on why it fits a beginner audience.
- **Script:** 0–3s hook · 3–10s the mistake · 10–22s the fix in 3 steps · 22–30s CTA.
- **Caption:** short caption + CTA + hashtags, plus one filming tip.
